country.title: Macro RBA Monitor
country.lede: What is Australia’s central bank dealing with right now, and what will it most likely do at its next meeting? This page explains it from the very beginning, in everyday language, one step at a time. You do not need any background in money or economics.

meeting.who: The Reserve Bank of Australia (“the RBA”), Australia’s central bank. Since 2025 its rate decisions are made by a nine-member Monetary Policy Board, chaired by Governor Michele Bullock. Members vote. The RBA publishes how many voted each way, but not who voted which way (an “unattributed” vote).

verdict.headline: HOLD
verdict.sub: Keep the cash rate where it is, at 4.60%. This remains a very close call ahead of the November 3 meeting.
verdict.confidence_note: “Low” means this is very close. September CPI came in at 4.3% and oil remains elevated, keeping a November rate rise on the table alongside the new Statement on Monetary Policy.
verdict.short_version: Australian consumer price inflation ticked up to 4.3% in September and oil prices have climbed further, while the RBA raised rates in late September. With a new Statement on Monetary Policy due on November 3, another rate rise is a very real possibility, but we think the RBA will likely pause to assess the full impact of its September move.
verdict.card_why: Inflation ticked up to 4.3% in September and oil prices rose, but the RBA only just moved in September; the November 3 decision is near.

why_steps.title: The RBA has two jobs, and one main tool
why_steps.html: By law, the RBA aims for price stability and full employment at the same time. For prices, its target is that inflation (the speed at which prices rise) stays between 2% and 3% a year, aiming for the middle, 2.5%. Its main tool is the cash rate: the interest rate banks charge each other to borrow money overnight. Banks pass changes in it on to variable-rate mortgages, business loans and savings accounts, usually within weeks. Think of it like the pedals of a car. Raising the rate is pressing the brake: loans get more expensive, so people and companies borrow and spend less, and prices cool down. Cutting the rate is pressing the gas. Holding means keeping your foot where it is. Because most Australian home loans are variable, the RBA’s brake reaches family budgets faster than in many other countries.

why_steps.title: Prices are clearly too high, and oil is making it worse
why_steps.html: The Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) says consumer prices were 4.3% higher in September than a year earlier, up from 4.0% in August (ABS). In simple terms: a basket of everyday things that cost A$100 a year ago now costs about A$104.30. The target would be about A$102.50. Part of the recent pressure comes from energy costs. Petrol and diesel prices rose 23.6% in September compared to a year earlier, up from 13.5% in August. Electricity prices remain elevated at 12.8%. At the same time, the RBA’s preferred underlying measure, the trimmed mean, sits at 3.6% for September. (The trimmed mean ignores the items with the biggest and smallest price changes each month, so one-offs like a fuel spike do not distort it.) It remains above the 2–3% target band.

why_steps.title: So the RBA has pressed the brake four times this year
why_steps.html: The RBA raised its rate in February (to 3.85%), March (4.10%), May (4.35%) and, most recently, on September 29 (to 4.60%). The September decision was unanimous. The RBA said “some of the upside risks flagged in August are materialising” and that “a further tightening in financial conditions is warranted” (RBA). Governor Bullock noted in her October 28 Senate testimony that inflation will likely be higher than previous forecasts due to energy price shocks and capacity pressures (RBA). There are two meetings left this year: November 2–3 and December 7–8. The upcoming meeting on November 3 coincides with the release of a new Statement on Monetary Policy containing the RBA’s updated forecasts.

why_steps.title: Reasons the RBA might wait
why_steps.html:
• It only just moved. The September 29 rate rise to 4.60% will barely have reached mortgage payments by the November meeting. The brake takes months to fully work through the economy.
  • Jobs are softening. Unemployment stood at 4.7% in September (ABS), and employment fell by 39,329 during the month.
  • Households are feeling the squeeze. The monthly household spending indicator registered 6.8% in August, national house prices remain below their peak, and mortgage payments take about 10% of household disposable income.
  • The bond market has tightened conditions. The 10-year Australian government bond rate is around 5.28%, which helps push up fixed-rate mortgages and business loan costs without requiring immediate central bank action.

why_steps.title: Reasons the RBA might raise rates again
why_steps.html:
• Inflation is above target and moving higher. September headline CPI reached 4.3% and the trimmed mean is at 3.6%, remaining well outside the 2–3% target band.
  • Oil prices have surged past assumptions. Brent oil reached $123.10 a barrel in late October, far above the RBA's August forecast assumption of US$81 by December.
  • New forecasts in November. The RBA publishes a fresh Statement on Monetary Policy with the November 3 decision. If updated forecasts show inflation staying elevated for longer, a rate rise becomes much easier to justify.
  • Capacity pressures. Governor Bullock stated in her Senate testimony that despite rising unemployment, the labour market remains tighter than previously judged, sustaining underlying price pressures.

why_steps.title: Weighing both sides

New forecasts due in the November Statement on Monetary Policy
Governor notes upside risks to inflation have materialised
Underlying trimmed mean inflation stuck at 3.6%
right: The RBA raised rates only five weeks ago

Cooling household spending and housing market
Risk of overtightening a slowing economy

why_steps.html: Both sides are strong. What keeps us leaning slightly toward Hold is the RBA’s usual preference to assess the lagged impact of its recent 0.25-point hike before moving again back-to-back, even as incoming inflation data provides clear ammunition for a raise. That is why our probabilities remain at 55% Hold, 42% Raise and 3% Cut.

why_steps.title: The decision ahead on November 2–3
why_steps.html: On Tuesday, November 3 at 2:30 p.m. AEDT, the RBA will announce its latest interest rate decision alongside its quarterly Statement on Monetary Policy. Following the release of September inflation data showing CPI at 4.3% and Brent oil trading around $123.10 a barrel, the central bank faces a very tight choice between pausing to evaluate previous hikes or taking further action to combat persistent price pressures.

timeline.title: The last cut: the cash rate fell to 3.60%
timeline.what: The RBA lowered its rate by 0.25 points to 3.60%. All members agreed. It was the third cut of 2025.
timeline.why: Inflation had come back inside the 2–3% band, so the RBA felt safe easing off the brake a little.
timeline.people: Variable-rate mortgage payments fell slightly. Savings accounts paid a little less.
timeline.because: the RBA paused to watch the effects. Within weeks, price data started to surprise on the high side.

timeline.title: Three holds, as inflation picks up again
timeline.what: The RBA held at 3.60% in September, November and December, all unanimously. In September it warned that “inflation in the September quarter may be higher than expected.” In November it said “Inflation has recently picked up”: the trimmed mean rose 1.0% in the quarter and 3.0% over the year. In December it said “the risks to inflation have tilted to the upside.”
timeline.why: Spending by households and businesses was recovering faster than expected, and the job market was still a little tight, so firms found it easier to raise prices.
timeline.people: Hopes of more rate cuts faded. Loan and savings rates stayed about the same.
timeline.because: by the new year the RBA felt it had to reverse course.

timeline.title: The first rise: up to 3.85%
timeline.what: The RBA raised its rate by 0.25 points to 3.85%. The statement said: “Today's policy decision was unanimous.”
timeline.why: Inflation “rose materially in the second half of 2025”, private demand grew faster than expected and the job market was a little tight. The RBA judged that part of the rise came from the economy running too hot, not from one-offs.
timeline.people: Variable mortgage repayments started rising again, only months after the 2025 cuts.
timeline.because: the RBA was already braking when a new shock arrived from overseas.

timeline.title: War in the Middle East, and a split vote: up to 4.10%
timeline.what: The RBA raised again, to 4.10%, citing among other things higher fuel prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East. The vote was close: 5 members for the rise, 4 for holding at 3.85%.
timeline.why: When oil gets expensive, petrol, diesel, freight, flights and farm costs all rise. The RBA said the risks to inflation had “tilted further to the upside.” The four members who wanted to wait likely preferred to see the effect of February’s rise first (the statement does not give their reasons).
timeline.people: Two rate rises in six weeks, plus dearer petrol. Families with big mortgages felt the squeeze from both sides.
timeline.because: the RBA faced a question that would last all year: is the oil shock spreading into other prices?

timeline.title: A third rise: up to 4.35%
timeline.what: The RBA raised to 4.35%, with 8 members for and 1 for holding. It said the oil shock was showing early signs of feeding into wider price-setting, and that “inflation is likely to remain above target for some time.”
timeline.why: Monthly consumer prices had been running between about 4% and 4.6% a year in the spring months (ABS). The RBA’s forecasts assumed the conflict would be resolved soon and fuel prices would fall.
timeline.people: The cash rate was now back to where it was in 2024. A 0.25-point rise adds very roughly A$100 a month to the repayments on a A$600,000 variable home loan (our rough arithmetic).
timeline.because: after three rises in four meetings, the RBA chose to stop and see how hard the brake was biting.

timeline.title: Two pauses at 4.35%, as the economy cools
timeline.what: The RBA held twice, both times unanimously. In August it said labour market conditions had eased by more than expected and that “The disruption to global oil supply is adding directly to inflation.” The minutes show members weighed a rise against a hold and chose to take “time to assess the incoming data”. National house prices were about 1½% below their March peak.
timeline.why: Spending was slowing, housing was cooling and inflation in the June quarter came in a little below the RBA’s forecast. The RBA judged its rate was already “somewhat restrictive” (pressing the brake).
timeline.people: A breather for borrowers. In August, financial markets saw only about a 50% chance of one more rise by the end of 2026.
timeline.because: the RBA set a clear test: it would raise again only if the upside risks it was worried about actually happened.

timeline.title: Slower growth, steady pay, jobs softening
timeline.what: Wages (the Wage Price Index) rose 3.2% over the year to June. The economy grew 0.4% in the June quarter and 2.1% over the year. Unemployment stood at 4.7% in August.
timeline.people: Household saving edged up to 6.5% of income: people are being a bit more careful with money.
timeline.because: the economy looked cooler, but not weak enough to stop the RBA if inflation worsened.

timeline.title: The fourth rise: up to 4.60%
timeline.what: The RBA raised by 0.25 points to 4.60%, unanimously. It said “The conflict in the Middle East has broadened and global energy prices are now much higher than had been assumed” in August. The minutes say all members agreed; members only “briefly considered” holding.
timeline.why: Upside risks were “materialising”: local petrol and diesel prices were 13% above the August forecast, and underlying inflation was surprising on the high side, which the RBA put down partly to the economy running hot.
timeline.people: The Governor said: “I know this decision is difficult for households with a mortgage and businesses with loans”. Savings accounts and term deposits should pay a little more.
timeline.because: the next month’s price report showed why the RBA remained concerned.

timeline.title: September CPI rises to 4.3% and Governor testifies in Senate
timeline.what: The ABS reported September CPI inflation at 4.3%, with automotive fuel prices jumping 23.6%. Meanwhile, Governor Michele Bullock told the Senate Economics Legislation Committee that inflation will likely remain elevated above previous forecasts due to global energy shocks and domestic capacity pressures.
timeline.people: Higher energy costs continue to press on household budgets while mortgage rates remain at 4.60%.
timeline.because: our reading ahead of the November 2–3 meeting is that a rate hold is most likely, but another rate hike remains a realistic possibility.

choices.title: Hold: keep the cash rate at 4.60%
choices.meaning: the RBA keeps its foot where it is on the brake while assessing the impact of September's rate rise and reviewing the new Statement on Monetary Policy.
for: The September rise needs time. It has only been five weeks since the RBA moved to 4.60%.
Unemployment is rising. 4.7% in September, with employment falling by 39,329.
Households are slowing down. Spending indicators and cooling housing markets show monetary policy is biting.
December is close. Holding in November allows the RBA to absorb the full new forecast before deciding on any further moves.
against: Inflation is rising. Headline CPI ticked up to 4.3% in September and trimmed mean remains at 3.6%.
Oil has spiked further. Brent oil near $123 a barrel adds sustained cost pressures.
Governor's testimony. Governor Bullock noted that upside risks have materialised and inflation will likely be higher than August base-case forecasts.
choices.everyday: variable mortgage repayments and savings rates would stay roughly where they are for now, with attention shifting to December.

choices.title: Raise: up 0.25 points, to 4.85%
choices.meaning: the RBA presses the brake again in November to respond to higher-than-expected September inflation and surging oil prices.
for: Inflation came in higher. September CPI rose to 4.3%, remaining well above the 2–3% target band.
Energy shock. Automotive fuel prices surged 23.6% and Brent oil is trading near $123 a barrel.
New forecasts. The November Statement on Monetary Policy may show inflation returning to target later than previously anticipated.
Capacity pressures. The RBA noted that the labour market remains somewhat tight despite rising unemployment.
against: Too soon after September. Delivering back-to-back rate hikes before seeing the full lagged effect of the previous move is unusual for the current board.
Slowing labour market. Employment fell significantly in September, pointing to a cooling economy.
choices.everyday: variable mortgage repayments would rise by roughly A$100 a month on a A$600,000 loan, and savings accounts would pay slightly more.

choices.title: Cut: lower the cash rate
choices.meaning: the RBA would switch from the brake to the gas, reversing its recent policy stance.
for: Only in an extreme economic or financial shock.
against: Inflation is moving the wrong way. With CPI at 4.3% and oil prices surging, cutting rates would add fuel to price pressures.
The RBA just raised rates in September.
choices.everyday: loans would get cheaper, but such a move would signal severe economic distress.

change.lead: Our 55% / 42% / 3% probability split reflects the delicate balance between sticky inflation, surging oil prices, and a softening labour market ahead of the November 2–3 meeting and new Statement on Monetary Policy.
change.intro: The RBA reviews all available data before each decision. Reports released right before November 3 directly shape the upcoming verdict, while subsequent releases feed into the December meeting.

international_trade_price_inde.trigger: A sharp jump in import costs reinforces upside risks to inflation.

producer_price_indexes.trigger: Elevated producer prices support a hawkish stance.

building_approvals.trigger: Weaker approvals confirm the economy is cooling.

household_spending_indicator.why: Provides monthly insight into consumer demand.

other: Oil and energy markets. Brent oil at $123.10 a barrel keeps pressure on transport and production costs.
Global central banks. The U.S. Federal Reserve rate at 4.00% and ECB deposit rate at 2.50% show global monetary policy remains restrictive.
RBA communication. Governor Bullock's Senate testimony on October 28 highlighted that upside risks to inflation have materialised.

report_card.one: Headline CPI rose to 4.3% in September, remaining well above the RBA’s 2–3% target band.
report_card.look: Monthly consumer prices (CPI at 4.3%), trimmed mean inflation (3.6%), and automotive fuel prices (23.6%).
report_card.why: Inflation remains above target, driven by automotive fuel, electricity, and persistent services inflation.
report_card.change: Trimmed mean inflation falling sustainably back toward the 2–3% band and oil prices dropping significantly.
report_card.matters: This is why the RBA raised rates in September and remains on alert for further tightening.

report_card.one: Unemployment is at 4.7% and employment fell in September, showing signs of a cooling labour market.
report_card.look: Unemployment rate (4.7%), employment change (−39,329), and participation rate (66.8%).
report_card.why: While employment dropped in September, the RBA notes that capacity pressures and underlying labour market tightness persist.
report_card.change: Unemployment rising toward 5% (red) or falling back solidly with strong job creation (green).
report_card.matters: The softening job market provides the main reason for the RBA to consider pausing.

report_card.one: The economy is growing at a modest pace as households tighten spending.
report_card.look: Real GDP growth (0.4% in Q2), household consumption, and retail spending indicators.
report_card.why: Growth is slowing as intended by higher interest rates, though business investment remains relatively resilient.
report_card.change: A sharp deterioration in spending or weak GDP data moving growth to red.
report_card.matters: The RBA wants demand to moderate without causing a severe economic downturn.

report_card.one: Borrowing costs remain elevated in line with RBA rate hikes and firm bond yields.
report_card.look: 10-year government bond rate (5.28%), 2-year government bond rate (4.92%), and the Australian dollar (US$0.7034).
report_card.why: Financial conditions are restrictive, helping to cool demand even without immediate central bank action.
report_card.change: A disorderly surge in yields or sharp currency depreciation moving conditions to red.
report_card.matters: Higher market rates reinforce monetary policy tightening.

consumer_price_index_cpi_all_items.what: the ABS checks the prices of the things households buy, like food, rent, petrol and power, and compares them with a year ago. A 4.3% rise means a A$100 basket now costs about A$104.30.
consumer_price_index_cpi_all_items.why: the RBA’s 2–3% target is defined on this measure. It ticked up to 4.3% in September from 4.0% in August.

trimmed_mean_inflation_monthly.what: each month the ABS sets aside the items with the biggest and smallest price changes and averages the rest to strip out one-offs.
trimmed_mean_inflation_monthly.why: the RBA’s favourite gauge of underlying inflation sits at 3.6% in September, remaining above the target band.

cpi_excluding_volatile_items_and_holid.what: all prices except fruit, vegetables, fuel and holiday travel, which jump around a lot.
cpi_excluding_volatile_items_and_holid.why: stands at 3.6% in September, showing underlying price pressures across the broader economy.

automotive_fuel_prices.what: the price of petrol and diesel at the bowser.
automotive_fuel_prices.why: surged 23.6% in September due to higher world oil prices, feeding directly into broader transport and freight costs.

electricity_prices.why: stands at 12.8% in September, continuing to add pressure to household budgets.

rents.why: holding at 3.6% in September, reflecting steady housing cost pressures.

services_vs_goods_inflation.what: the CPI split into physical goods and services like haircuts and meals out.
services_vs_goods_inflation.why: services inflation at +3.7% and goods at +4.2% show widespread price pressures.

quarterly_cpi_and_trimmed_mean.what: the price rise measured over the whole quarter.
quarterly_cpi_and_trimmed_mean.why: stood at CPI +3.9% and trimmed mean +3.6% in the June quarter per RBA reports.

rba_forecast_when_inflation_returns_to.what: the RBA's forecast for inflation to return to the midpoint of the 2–3% target range.
rba_forecast_when_inflation_returns_to.why: August forecasts projected a return by early 2028, though recent energy shocks may push timelines out.

unemployment_rate.what: the share of people who want a job and are looking, but do not have one.
unemployment_rate.why: stands at 4.7% in September, in line with expectations of a gradual labour market easing.

employment_change.what: how many more people had a job than the month before.
employment_change.why: employment fell by 39,329 in September, pointing to a softer hiring month.

participation_rate.what: the share of adults who are working or looking for work.
participation_rate.why: stands at 66.8% in September, showing robust labor force attachment.

employment_to_population_ratio.what: the share of all adults who have a job.
employment_to_population_ratio.why: stands at 63.6% in September, indicating solid overall employment levels.

underemployment_rate.what: people who have a job but want more hours.
underemployment_rate.why: stands at 6.3% in September, showing mild slack in the labour market.

wage_price_index.what: how fast pay rates for the same jobs are rising.
wage_price_index.why: at 3.2% in Q2 2026, wage growth remains moderate relative to headline inflation.

rba_forecast_unemployment.what: the RBA's expected path for unemployment.
rba_forecast_unemployment.why: forecasts project 4.5% by Dec 2026 and 4.8% by end-2028.

abs_caution_on_recent_data.what: ABS advisory on interpreting short-term survey moves with care.
abs_caution_on_recent_data.why: reminds analysts not to overreact to single-month labour force volatility.

real_gdp_growth.what: total economic output adjusted for inflation.
real_gdp_growth.why: grew 0.4% in Q2 2026, indicating slow but positive economic growth.

household_consumption.what: spending by households on goods and services.
household_consumption.why: grew 0.4% in Q2 2026, reflecting cautious consumer behavior.

household_spending_indicator.what: monthly measure of household spending from bank-card data.
household_spending_indicator.why: stood at 6.8% in August, showing ongoing spending activity.

household_saving_ratio.what: share of after-tax income that households save.
household_saving_ratio.why: stood at 6.5% in Q2 2026, showing households are setting aside more cash.

terms_of_trade.why: stood at -1.6% in Q2 2026 as dearer imported energy weighs on trade returns.

new_housing_loan_commitments_owner_occ.what: new home loans agreed by lenders for owner-occupiers.
new_housing_loan_commitments_owner_occ.why: fell 3.3% in the June quarter, showing housing finance reacting to higher interest rates.

national_house_prices.what: private house price index summary described by the RBA.
national_house_prices.why: stood about 1½% below the March peak by August, reflecting cooling property markets.

business_investment.what: spending by firms on machinery, buildings and technology.
business_investment.why: up more than 10% over the year, supporting overall economic demand.

rba_cash_rate_target.what: the RBA's target for the overnight cash rate.
rba_cash_rate_target.why: stands at 4.60% following the September 29 rate increase.

market_pricing_for_more_rises.what: traders' expectations for future RBA rate moves.
market_pricing_for_more_rises.why: pricing implies further rate rises into late 2026 and early 2027.

10_year_government_bond_rate.what: interest rate paid on 10-year Australian government debt.
10_year_government_bond_rate.why: stands at 5.28% in October, keeping long-term borrowing costs elevated.

2_year_government_bond_rate.why: stands at 4.92% in October, reflecting expectations of firm monetary policy.

10_year_bond_rate_monthly_average.what: official monthly average of the 10-year bond yield.
10_year_bond_rate_monthly_average.why: averaged 5.28% in September, confirming elevated long-term yields.

3_month_bank_bill_rate.what: rate banks pay to borrow from each other for three months.
3_month_bank_bill_rate.why: stands at 4.67% in September, closely tracking the cash rate.

australian_dollar.what: exchange rate of the Australian dollar against the U.S. dollar.
australian_dollar.why: stands at US$0.7034 on October 28, helping moderate import price pressures.

mortgage_payments_vs_income.what: scheduled mortgage repayments as a share of household disposable income.
mortgage_payments_vs_income.why: stands at about 10%, reflecting the financial burden of higher interest rates.

oil_price_brent.what: world benchmark price of crude oil.
oil_price_brent.why: stands at $123.10 a barrel on October 27, significantly above RBA forecast assumptions.

rba_oil_assumption_august.what: oil price assumption built into RBA August forecasts.
rba_oil_assumption_august.why: assumed Brent near US$81 by December, creating a wide gap with current market prices.

u_s_federal_reserve_rate_top_of_range.what: upper end of the U.S. Federal Reserve target range.
u_s_federal_reserve_rate_top_of_range.why: stands at 4.00%, influencing global financial conditions.

ecb_deposit_rate.what: main policy interest rate of the euro area.
ecb_deposit_rate.why: stands at 2.50%, showing global central banks addressing similar pressures.

australian_share_prices.what: summary of the Australian stock market.

said.v: Governor Bullock notes inflation will likely be higher than August forecasts
w: What it said: “Developments since then suggest that although growth in the Australian economy is slowing as expected, some of the international and domestic upside risks to inflation have materialised or are materialising. Inflation will therefore likely be higher than was our base case in August.”
Why it matters: confirms that recent energy shocks and capacity pressures are keeping pressure on the RBA to maintain a restrictive policy stance.
What it said: “Inflation remains elevated and some of the upside risks flagged in August are materialising.” It will act “including increasing the cash rate target further if needed.”
Why it matters: the door to more rises remains open.

What it said: “Members briefly considered the arguments in support of leaving the cash rate target unchanged.” Arguments to hold “rested primarily on the possibility that downside risks to activity and employment could prove larger than expected.”
Why it matters: highlights that job market conditions remain the primary counterweight against further rate hikes.

said.v: “The Board will increase interest rates again if that's what's needed to get inflation down.”
w: What it said: also “I'm not going to give you forward guidance” and acknowledging that households with a mortgage are facing difficulties.
Why it matters: signals that future decisions depend strictly on incoming data without pre-committed schedules.
What it said: “The disruption to global oil supply is adding directly to inflation”; inflation is “not expected to return to around the midpoint of the target range until late 2027”.
Why it matters: established the conditional test that led to September's rate hike when risks materialised.

said.v: Feb 9–0 · Mar 5–4 · May 8–1 · Jun 9–0 · Aug 9–0 · Sep 9–0
w: What it is: how many of the nine members voted for each decision.
Why it matters: illustrates broad board consensus following the tight March vote.

gaps: Market odds specifically for November. Official market pricing reflects expectations out to year-end and early 2027, but exact daily probabilities for the November meeting alone are estimated.
Daily government bond yields. Current 10-year (5.28%) and 2-year (4.92%) yields are drawn from secondary financial market data sources rather than direct RBA tables.
Detailed survey breakdowns of inflation expectations. While the RBA notes short-term expectations remain elevated, detailed household and business survey datasets were not fully collected.

group_intros.prices: These numbers tell us how fast things are getting more expensive. The RBA aims to keep inflation between 2% and 3% a year, ideally at 2.5%. It watches the “trimmed mean”, which removes the jumpiest prices, to see the underlying trend.
group_intros.jobs: These numbers tell us how easy it is to find work, and how fast pay is rising. The RBA’s second job is full employment, and a tight job market can push up wages and prices.
group_intros.growth: These numbers tell us how fast the economy is growing and whether households are still spending. A slower economy usually means less pressure on prices.
group_intros.rates: These numbers show the RBA’s own rate and the interest rates in financial markets, which decide what households and firms actually pay to borrow.
group_intros.said: RBA officials often hint at what they will do next. Reading their words carefully is one of the best ways to guess the next decision.
group_intros.global: Australia trades heavily with the world and imports most of its fuel, so world oil prices and other central banks matter.

copy.story_intro: This is the story of the past year, in order. Each step explains what happened, why it happened, and what it meant for ordinary people. The line at the bottom of each step (“Because of this…”) shows how it led to the next step, so you can follow cause and effect from start to finish.
copy.choices_intro: At every meeting the RBA has three options. Below we explain what each one would mean, why it could happen, why it might not, and what it would mean in everyday life. Analysis · our judgement
copy.report_intro: Think of this as a school report for the economy in four subjects. Green means healthy. Yellow means mixed, keep watching. Red means a problem the central bank must fix. Each grade is also written in words, so you do not need to see the color. Analysis
copy.gaps_intro: Good research is honest about its blind spots. Here is what is missing, delayed or unverified, and why it matters.
copy.numbers_intro: Every number we used, grouped by topic. For each one you will see the latest value, the period it covers, when it was published, the previous value, where it came from, and, most importantly, a plain explanation of what it is and why it matters. Tap a group to open or close it. Observed facts

live_before.html: The numbers on this page are a snapshot taken on October 14, 2026. If you want to see whether anything has changed since then, you can try loading the newest values from FRED, a free public data service run by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Note: FRED does not carry an up-to-date Australian consumer price series (its OECD copy stops in early 2025), so for prices use the ABS directly. Most Australian series on FRED are monthly or quarterly averages copied from the OECD with a delay of several weeks, so they may differ from the daily and latest figures on this page.

How it works: FRED gives anyone a free “API key”, a code that works like a library card for its data. Paste your key below and press Refresh. The newest values appear in a separate table, next to our snapshot values so you can compare. The rest of this page stays exactly as it is.
Privacy: your key is saved only in this browser, on this device, and is sent only to FRED. Press “Forget key” to remove it. Get a free key at fred.stlouisfed.org.

live_after.html: Good to know: FRED often does not allow web pages to request its data directly, so many browsers will block this. If that happens, you will see a clear message and nothing on the page will change. You can always check the same numbers yourself on the FRED website.

summary.headline: Headline CPI inflation rose to 4.3% in September from 4.0% in August, while monthly trimmed mean inflation held at 3.6%.
items: Consumer Price Index (CPI) rose from 4.0% in August to 4.3% in September (annual rate).
Trimmed mean inflation held steady at 3.6% in September compared to August.
Automotive fuel prices jumped sharply from 13.5% in August to 23.6% in September due to higher world oil prices.
Oil price (Brent) increased to $123.10 a barrel on October 27 from $115.22 on October 20.

Governor Michele Bullock delivered her opening statement to the Senate Economics Legislation Committee on October 28, noting that inflation will likely be higher than the RBA's August forecasts due to materialising upside risks.
